lines.text: What if Africa split in two?
It already is: Africa's two plates pull apart by 8 to 9 millimetres a year.
It starts in Ethiopia's Afar desert and runs south as one long line, the East African Rift, past Lake Turkana, through Kenya and into Tanzania.
That's slow, far too slow to feel. So what happens if it never stops?
First, the sea breaks in through the Red Sea's southern end and floods the Afar, which already lies lower than the sea in places.
Then where does the water go? It follows the crack south, through Ethiopia and Kenya, and a brand-new coastline is drawn on both sides.
On this simplified map, everything to the east, Somalia, eastern Ethiopia and Kenya, and Tanzania's coast, breaks off as one giant island, drifting out into the Indian Ocean.
And here is the twist: Ethiopia, a country with no sea today, wakes up with a coast and a harbour of its own, on a sea that does not exist yet.
How long would it take? Tens of millions of years. But one crack opened fast: in 2005, 60 kilometres of the Afar tore open in a matter of days, some cracks more than a metre wide.
New island or new coast: which side would you pick? Tell us below. Because one day, Africa may split in two.
